title: Count the stars (Genesis 15:1–6)
hookLine: childless and old, Abram is told to look up and count the stars

cards: A vision comes to Abram, and God speaks. In the old JPS translation: "Fear not, Abram, I am thy shield, thy reward shall be exceeding great." And Abram, who so far in the story has mostly just obeyed, answers back.
What will you give me? I'm going childless. The heir of my house is my steward, Eliezer of Damascus.
You've given me no children. It's the voice of anyone who has been promised something for years and is starting to stop believing it: a job, a family, a recovery, a change.
What good is a great reward, if the thing I actually want never comes? God doesn't argue. God takes him outside.

teach.b: Outside, under the whole sky, God says: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." And then: "So shall thy seed be."
On a clear desert night, with no city lights and no haze, the sky is thick with stars, too many to count. That's the point.
The task is impossible. It isn't a math problem; it's a way of making an old man tip his head back and look up. The rabbis had fun with this.
The Talmud imagines Abram saying: I've read my own stars, and they say I won't have a son. And God answers: step outside your astrology.
You are not bound by the stars. Another midrash says God lifted Abram up above the stars, so that he looked down on them. Either way, the sky that seemed to say no becomes a yes.
Then comes one short verse: "And he believed in the LORD; and He counted it to him for righteousness." The word for believed shares a root with amen, a root that has to do with being firm.
And the word for righteousness is tzedakah, from tzedek, the word you met with Noah.
In the English, count appears twice: Abram is told to count the stars, and, in the most common reading, God counts his trust as righteousness. He couldn't finish counting. He didn't have to.
He looked up, and he leaned on the promise.

how: Jews read this vision in the Torah portion Lech Lecha, and the verse "he believed in the LORD; and He counted it to him for righteousness" is often studied as the Torah's first picture of emunah, faith as trust.

o: a reward God pays for obeying
faith that never asks God questions

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Abram quietly accepts God's promise of a reward
he answers back: what will you give me, since I go childless?
the Talmud imagines God telling Abram he isn't bound by the stars
Abram says his stars show no son; God tells him to step outside his astrology.
God expects Abram to finish counting
the task is impossible on purpose. it makes him look up.

games.q: you're Abram, old and childless, and God has promised you a great reward. what do you say?
o: what will you give me, when I have no child?
games.why: he answers back honestly. God takes him outside and tells him to count the stars: so shall thy seed be.

practice: If you can, close your eyes and picture the darkest night sky you've ever seen, at a campsite, a beach, a field far from town, and let the stars fill in, one by one, until there are too many.
Bring to mind one promise you're still waiting on, or one hope that feels old, and don't solve it; just hold it under that sky. If you pray, you can lean on it there.

wordCard.voice: Tzedakah, the Hebrew word for righteousness, counted to Abram for believing God's promise under a sky too thick with stars to number.

orig.note: Hebrew: stars. the singular is kochav.

carryVoice: Your line: look up and count. The stars are still too many to number. See you tomorrow.
